tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
and `harness/` only through two doors: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` (facts only, each
sourced) and `docs/HARNESS.md` (the harness as a black box). Everything else
the firmware side can read, so spec-side commit messages, pull request
titles and descriptions, and every file outside those two folders and
`sessions/spec/` (docs, tools, tests, records, release notes) describe what
changed in general terms, never emulator internals: no register names,
addresses, struct or function names, or code excerpts. Such detail goes in
comments inside `harness/`. CI logs and records from harness runs show
results (pass/fail, hashes, images, numbers), never emulator source.
`tools/check-emulator-terms.py` (C-SEP-TERMS) looks for identifiers that
occur only in `vendor/emulator/` in all of those places and reports a hit
by place and hash, never the word; run it (with `--show`, in a spec folder)
on your commit messages before you push. People review the two doors, so a
term that occurs in either of them as merged on main is accepted everywhere
(read from main's commit, never the working tree: a term a branch adds to a
door is still a hit until that change has merged). Other reviewed false
positives are listed by hash in `config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json`.

## Commit messages

Every commit follows `.gitmessage` (run `tools/install-hooks.sh` once to make
it git's template and turn on the commit-msg hook):

```
<area>: <what changed, one line>

What:    what this commit does
Why:     the reason (the milestone and requirement IDs it serves)
How:     the approach, and anything tried and rejected
Result:  what the author saw when testing (the CI record is the authoritative result)
Sources: PROVENANCE IDs used (or "none")
Exposure: the author's role and exposure (e.g. "firmware side, none")
```

- `<area>` is lower-case: `docs`, `tools`, `ci`, `firmware`, `vendor`,
  `config`, `sessions`, and so on.
- A field may continue on following lines, indented.
- Agent-written commits end with the trailers `Model: <exact model ID>` and
  `Claude-Session: <session URL>` (and `Co-Authored-By:`). Their author is
  the agent; the owner is the committer.
- Small commits: one idea each.
- Merge commits are exempt from the template; the pull request they merge
  carries the sections.

`tools/check-commit-msg.py` enforces this in the hook and in CI (C-COMMIT-MSG).

## Pull requests and merging

- Agents and contributors commit **unsigned** on branches and open a pull
  request using `.github/pull_request_template.md` (the same sections, plus
  links to the CI run and the record).
- CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) must pass.
- The **owner merges with GitHub's merge button** ("Create a merge commit").
  GitHub commits and signs the merge commit as `web-flow` (shown as
  Verified) and records the owner as the pull request's `merged_by`. No
  squash or rebase merges, and nobody bypasses the rules.
- Records (`records/<sha>/` on the `records` branch) are written only by
  `.github/workflows/records.yml`, for pushes to main, and the similarity
  audit's report beside it (`records/<sha>/audit/`) only by
  `.github/workflows/audit.yml`'s record job (docs/AUDIT.md). Both use the
  `records` environment's deploy key.
- **Performance budgets** (`config/budgets.json`, R-PERF-1) are raised, or
  moved to the next milestone's, only by a pull request of their own that
  says why in the What/Why/How/Result sections and changes nothing else.
  When CI's performance summary shows an improvement of more than 3%
  (R-PERF-2), say so in the pull request's Result.
- Milestones end with a tag `mN`, signed by the owner with their SSH key
  (below), and a GitHub release with the build outputs, the record and an
  SBOM.

### Merge policy and its history

- **2026-10-21:** the owner first chose to sign every merge with their own
  SSH key, as the ruleset's only bypass actor, because GitHub's button signs
  with GitHub's key instead.
- **2026-10-22:** pull request #1 was merged with the button. Its merge
  commit `2fd28219` is signed by GitHub (`web-flow`, verified), and its
  record shows C-MERGE **FAIL** under the old rule ("committer is web-flow,
  not the owner"). The record stays as it is, and history is not rewritten.
- **2026-10-22:** the owner then chose button merges for good. The bypass
  was removed from the main ruleset, so the rules now apply to everyone.

What a merge on main proves: GitHub's signature shows the commit was made
by GitHub on the owner's merge. `merged_by` shows the owner pressed the
button. The required `ci` check shows CI passed on exactly the merged head.
The records workflow re-checks all of this for every push to main
(C-MERGE): a merge commit, a verified signature, committer `web-flow` with
the pull request's `merged_by` the owner (or, for older merges, the owner
as committer), and its second parent the head of a pull request whose `ci`
run passed. Otherwise the record says **FAIL** for C-MERGE, and the record
is still written.

## Rulesets

Repository rulesets (Settings → Rules → Rulesets):

- **main**: restrict deletions; block force pushes; require a pull request
  before merging (allowed merge method: merge only); require status checks to
  pass (the `ci` job); no bypass (until 2026-10-22: the repository admin
  role).
- **records-history** (branch `records`): restrict deletions; block force
  pushes; no bypass.
- **records-writer** (branch `records`): restrict creations; restrict
  updates; bypass list: deploy keys only. Together these make the records
  workflow's deploy key the only writer, and it can only add commits.
- **milestone-tags** (tags `m*`): restrict deletions; restrict updates; no
  bypass.

Repository settings: allow merge commits only (squash and rebase merging
off).

Set up on 2026-10-22 by session M0a, with the owner's approval, through the
GitHub API:

| What | ID or fingerprint |
|------|-------------------|
| Ruleset `main` | 25612787 (required check `ci` from GitHub Actions; no bypass since 2026-10-22, before that the repository admin role) |
| Ruleset `records-history` | 25612788 |
| Ruleset `records-writer` | 25612790 (bypass: deploy keys) |
| Ruleset `milestone-tags` | 25612791 |
| Environment `records` | deployments from `main` only; secret `RECORDS_DEPLOY_KEY` |
| Deploy key "records workflow (records branch writer)" | 167260041, write access, ED25519 `SHA256:Od9RfSkzLwqLYSZRf1X7jEdcLhty0n1ISgQ+ec43Dkk` |

The deploy key's private half was generated in the session's scratch
folder, piped into the environment secret without being printed, and
deleted. To rotate it: make a new pair, replace the secret, add the new
public key, delete the old key.

## SSH signing for milestone tags (one-time setup, owner)

1. Create a signing key (or reuse an SSH key you already have):
   `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "small-beeps signing" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing`
2. Tell git to sign with it:
   ```sh
   git config --global gpg.format ssh
   git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing.pub
   git config --global tag.gpgSign true
   ```
   Leave `commit.gpgSign` off: merges are signed by GitHub's button.
3. Let git verify signatures locally: add a line
   `<your git email> <contents of id_ed25519_signing.pub>` to
   `~/.ssh/allowed_signers`, then
   `git config --global gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile ~/.ssh/allowed_signers`.
4. On GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → Key type
   **Signing Key**, and paste the `.pub` contents.
5. Tag a milestone: `git tag -s mN -m "mN"`, then `git push origin mN`.
6. Check: `git tag -v mN` shows "Good "git" signature", and GitHub shows the
   tag as **Verified**.

## Licences

- Every file we write starts with an SPDX header:
  `SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT` and `SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98`.
  Files that can't carry one are covered in `REUSE.toml`.
- Vendored files keep their own licences (`vendor/*/LICENSE`, `NOTICE`).
- CI runs `reuse lint` and fails on any gap (C-REUSE).
- Never commit the toolchain or anything containing it (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md).
- Nothing secret ever goes in: no keys, tokens or private notes. The
  repository is public and history is never rewritten.

## Privacy

The repository is public. No committed file, commit message or pull request
text names the owner's username, real name, e-mail address, hostname or
local folder names, or a full local path: write paths relative to the
repository, or as `~/...` with the top folder shown as `<top>`. Anyone who
finds such a term in the repository tells the owner instead of repeating it.

- **The terms** are kept by the owner, never in the repository: in the
  gitignored `tools/[REDACTED:host]` (one per line, `#` comments,
  matched ignoring case) and in the repository secret `PRIVATE_TERMS`, which
  CI passes to the check.
- **The check** `tools/check-private.py` (C-PRIVATE, R-PUB-3) scans every
  tracked file and every commit message, and the pre-commit and commit-msg
  hooks scan staged files and the message (`tools/install-hooks.sh` turns
  them on). A hit is reported by file and line only, never the term. CI
  fails when the secret is missing.
- **Records are scanned too** (since M1). Before a test record, an audit
  report or a C-MERGE re-check is hashed, uploaded or pushed, any file in
  it holding a term is withheld: deleted, and listed with the SHA-256 of
  the original in `WITHHELD.json`, which the record keeps (C-RECORD-PRIVATE).
  The original is not kept anywhere; the checks are deterministic, so it
  can be regenerated and matched to its hash. CI artifacts are kept 14 days.
- **Older records stay as they are.** A file under `sessions/` or
  `docs/prompts/` whose blob is identical to the same path at the base
  commit in `config/private-base` (the last main commit before the check)
  is exempt. This is decided from git's object hashes alone, so no session
  opens or lists the spec side's transcripts for it, and the check prints
  only how many files it exempted per folder. Every file added or changed
  after the base is checked in full. Files that sessions keep editing get no
  exemption: their current text is redacted instead (`docs/EXPOSURE.md` was,
  on 2026-10-22), and git history keeps the originals.
- **Archived transcripts** are redacted by `tools/archive-session.py`: the
  username anywhere it appears, the local top-level folder as `<top>`, and
  every private term.

## Low profile (for now)

The repository is public but unpromoted. In its name, description and topics,
and in README.md, never use these quiet words: **FM-1, M-VAVE, JieLi, synth,
firmware** (any spelling or case; `tools/check-low-profile.py` has the
patterns). Don't link the repository from anywhere, star it, fork it or
announce it. Everything else in the repository stays complete and truthful.
docs/GOING-PUBLIC.md says how this ends.

by place and hash, never the word; run it (with `--show`, in a spec folder)
on your commit messages before you push. People review the two doors, so a
term that occurs in either of them as merged on main is accepted everywhere
(read from main's commit, never the working tree: a term a branch adds to a
door is still a hit until that change has merged). Other reviewed false
positives are listed by hash in `config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json`.

## Commit messages

Every commit follows `.gitmessage` (run `tools/install-hooks.sh` once to make
it git's template and turn on the commit-msg hook):

```
<area>: <what changed, one line>

What:    what this commit does
Why:     the reason (the milestone and requirement IDs it serves)
How:     the approach, and anything tried and rejected
Result:  what the author saw when testing (the CI record is the authoritative result)
Sources: PROVENANCE IDs used (or "none")
Exposure: the author's role and exposure (e.g. "firmware side, none")
```

- `<area>` is lower-case: `docs`, `tools`, `ci`, `firmware`, `vendor`,
  `config`, `sessions`, and so on.
- A field may continue on following lines, indented.
- Agent-written commits end with the trailers `Model: <exact model ID>` and
  `Claude-Session: <session URL>` (and `Co-Authored-By:`). Their author is
  the agent; the owner is the committer.
- Small commits: one idea each.
- Merge commits are exempt from the template; the pull request they merge
  carries the sections.

`tools/check-commit-msg.py` enforces this in the hook and in CI (C-COMMIT-MSG).

## Pull requests and merging

- Agents and contributors commit **unsigned** on branches and open a pull
  request using `.github/pull_request_template.md` (the same sections, plus
  links to the CI run and the record).
- CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) must pass.
- The **owner merges with GitHub's merge button** ("Create a merge commit").
  GitHub commits and signs the merge commit as `web-flow` (shown as
  Verified) and records the owner as the pull request's `merged_by`. No
  squash or rebase merges, and nobody bypasses the rules.
- Records (`records/<sha>/` on the `records` branch) are written only by
  `.github/workflows/records.yml`, for pushes to main, and the similarity
  audit's report beside it (`records/<sha>/audit/`) only by
  `.github/workflows/audit.yml`'s record job (docs/AUDIT.md). Both use the
  `records` environment's deploy key.
- **Performance budgets** (`config/budgets.json`, R-PERF-1) are raised, or
  moved to the next milestone's, only by a pull request of their own that
  says why in the What/Why/How/Result sections and changes nothing else.
  When CI's performance summary shows an improvement of more than 3%
  (R-PERF-2), say so in the pull request's Result.
- Milestones end with a tag `mN`, signed by the owner with their SSH key
  (below), and a GitHub release with the build outputs, the record and an
  SBOM.

### Merge policy and its history

- **2026-10-21:** the owner first chose to sign every merge with their own
  SSH key, as the ruleset's only bypass actor, because GitHub's button signs
  with GitHub's key instead.
- **2026-10-22:** pull request #1 was merged with the button. Its merge
  commit `2fd28219` is signed by GitHub (`web-flow`, verified), and its
  record shows C-MERGE **FAIL** under the old rule ("committer is web-flow,
  not the owner"). The record stays as it is, and history is not rewritten.
- **2026-10-22:** the owner then chose button merges for good. The bypass
  was removed from the main ruleset, so the rules now apply to everyone.

What a merge on main proves: GitHub's signature shows the commit was made
by GitHub on the owner's merge. `merged_by` shows the owner pressed the
button. The required `ci` check shows CI passed on exactly the merged head.
The records workflow re-checks all of this for every push to main
(C-MERGE): a merge commit, a verified signature, committer `web-flow` with
the pull request's `merged_by` the owner (or, for older merges, the owner
as committer), and its second parent the head of a pull request whose `ci`
run passed. Otherwise the record says **FAIL** for C-MERGE, and the record
is still written.

## Rulesets

Repository rulesets (Settings → Rules → Rulesets):

- **main**: restrict deletions; block force pushes; require a pull request
  before merging (allowed merge method: merge only); require status checks to
  pass (the `ci` job); no bypass (until 2026-10-22: the repository admin
  role).
- **records-history** (branch `records`): restrict deletions; block force
  pushes; no bypass.
- **records-writer** (branch `records`): restrict creations; restrict
  updates; bypass list: deploy keys only. Together these make the records
  workflow's deploy key the only writer, and it can only add commits.
- **milestone-tags** (tags `m*`): restrict deletions; restrict updates; no
  bypass.

Repository settings: allow merge commits only (squash and rebase merging
off).

## SSH signing for milestone tags (one-time setup, owner)

1. Create a signing key (or reuse an SSH key you already have):
   `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "small-beeps signing" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing`
2. Tell git to sign with it:
   ```sh
   git config --global gpg.format ssh
   git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing.pub
   git config --global tag.gpgSign true
   ```
   Leave `commit.gpgSign` off: merges are signed by GitHub's button.
3. Let git verify signatures locally: add a line
   `<your git email> <contents of id_ed25519_signing.pub>` to
   `~/.ssh/allowed_signers`, then
   `git config --global gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile ~/.ssh/allowed_signers`.
4. On GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → Key type
   **Signing Key**, and paste the `.pub` contents.
5. Tag a milestone: `git tag -s mN -m "mN"`, then `git push origin mN`.
6. Check: `git tag -v mN` shows "Good "git" signature", and GitHub shows the
   tag as **Verified**.

## Licences

- Every file we write starts with an SPDX header:
  `SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT` and `SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98`.
  Files that can't carry one are covered in `REUSE.toml`.
- Vendored files keep their own licences (`vendor/*/LICENSE`, `NOTICE`).
- CI runs `reuse lint` and fails on any gap (C-REUSE).
- Never commit the toolchain or anything containing it (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md).
- Nothing secret ever goes in: no keys, tokens or private notes. The
  repository is public and history is never rewritten.

## Privacy

The repository is public. No committed file, commit message or pull request
text names the owner's username, real name, e-mail address, hostname or
local folder names, or a full local path: write paths relative to the
repository, or as `~/...` with the top folder shown as `<top>`. Anyone who
finds such a term in the repository tells the owner instead of repeating it.

- **The terms** are kept by the owner, never in the repository: in the
  gitignored `tools/[REDACTED:host]` (one per line, `#` comments,
  matched ignoring case) and in the repository secret `PRIVATE_TERMS`, which
  CI passes to the check.
- **The check** `tools/check-private.py` (C-PRIVATE, R-PUB-3) scans every
  tracked file and every commit message, and the pre-commit and commit-msg
  hooks scan staged files and the message (`tools/install-hooks.sh` turns
  them on). A hit is reported by file and line only, never the term. CI
  fails when the secret is missing.
- **Records are scanned too** (since M1). Before a test record, an audit
  report or a C-MERGE re-check is hashed, uploaded or pushed, any file in
  it holding a term is withheld: deleted, and listed with the SHA-256 of
  the original in `WITHHELD.json`, which the record keeps (C-RECORD-PRIVATE).
  The original is not kept anywhere; the checks are deterministic, so it
  can be regenerated and matched to its hash. CI artifacts are kept 14 days.
- **Older records stay as they are.** A file under `sessions/` or
  `docs/prompts/` whose blob is identical to the same path at the base
  commit in `config/private-base` (the last main commit before the check)
  is exempt. This is decided from git's object hashes alone, so no session
  opens or lists the spec side's transcripts for it, and the check prints
  only how many files it exempted per folder. Every file added or changed
  after the base is checked in full. Files that sessions keep editing get no
  exemption: their current text is redacted instead (`docs/EXPOSURE.md` was,
  on 2026-10-22), and git history keeps the originals.
- **Archived transcripts** are redacted by `tools/archive-session.py`: the
  username anywhere it appears, the local top-level folder as `<top>`, and
  every private term.

## Low profile (for now)

The repository is public but unpromoted. In its name, description and topics,
and in README.md, never use these quiet words: **FM-1, M-VAVE, JieLi, synth,
firmware** (any spelling or case; `tools/check-low-profile.py` has the
patterns). Don't link the repository from anywhere, star it, fork it or
announce it. Everything else in the repository stays complete and truthful.
docs/GOING-PUBLIC.md says how this ends.

# Plan

An original, MIT-licensed base firmware for the M-VAVE FM-1 pocket
synthesizer (JieLi AC791N: two pi32v2 cores, 240x240 LCD, key matrix, rotary
encoders, I2S audio), written clean-room so it can ship inside the
F-Emulator iOS app, provably independent of the FM-1's GPL community
firmwares.

Each milestone has its own prompt (`docs/prompts/<Mx>.md`) and its own fresh
session. Roles are defined in CONTRIBUTING.md; requirement IDs are in
docs/REQUIREMENTS.md.

## Milestones

### M0a: foundation (firmware side)
Repo, rules, roles, exposure register, records, signing, toolchain, SDK, CI.
No firmware code yet; a placeholder translation unit proves the pipeline.
- Requirements: R-PROC-1..4, R-REC-1..2, R-REPRO-1..5, R-BUILD-1,
  R-LIC-1..2, R-PUB-1..2, R-CLEAN-1..5.
- Done when: the repo exists with the bootstrap commit and rulesets; CI on a
  pull request runs reuse lint, the commit-message check, the low-profile
  check, the toolchain container build with its checksum and the
  byte-for-byte double build; the owner's signed merge produces the first
  record with a pending OpenTimestamps proof; `tools/reproduce` works;
  EXPOSURE.md and PROVENANCE.md are complete; nothing forbidden was opened.
- Status 2026-10-22: pull request #1 merged as `2fd28219`. Its record
  (`records/2fd28219…/` on `records`) has 13 checks PASS and C-MERGE FAIL
  under the merge rule of the time (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Merge policy and its
  history"), with a pending OpenTimestamps proof (three calendars).
  `tools/reproduce 2fd28219` on the owner's Mac: REPRODUCED (both outputs
  match the record).

### M0b: harness (spec side)
Vendor the emulator crates `fm1-isa`, `fm1-core`, `fm1-soc` from the public
upstream `joakimeriksson/fm1-emu` at a pinned commit, with its MIT licence,
into `vendor/emulator/` (never the rest of that repo). Build the harness: a
Rust library and `fwtest` CLI that boots a raw image, runs N emulated ms with
a timed input script, captures RAM, the LCD (PNG), LEDs, flash, audio (WAV)
and instructions per audio block, detects halts, compares golden files, and
emits JUnit and JSON.
- Requirements: R-REPRO-*, R-LIC-*, new harness requirements (R-HARN-*).
- Done when: `fwtest` runs in CI from a pinned container, its outputs are
  deterministic, and `tools/clean-setup.sh` excludes `vendor/emulator/` and
  `harness/` from clean clones.
- Status 2026-10-22 (session M0b, spec side, on the owner's Mac):
  - **Setup** (pull request #3): the spec folder, its hand-made settings kept
    and guarded, M0a's transcripts archived in `sessions/clean/`; spec-side
    transcripts go to `sessions/spec/`, which clean folders leave out and
    deny (R-SEP-2).
  - **Emulator** (pull request #4): three crates vendored at upstream commit
    `43ed5580`, reproducible by `tools/fetch-emulator.sh` with a tree hash
    (C-EMU-PIN). One patch, to the workspace manifest only.
  - **Harness** (pull request #4): `fwtest`, a Rust library and CLI with no
    third-party crates, built offline in a container on digest-pinned bases
    (Rust 1.99.0). It boots raw images, takes timed inputs, captures RAM,
    the LCD (PNG), LEDs, flash, audio (WAV), instructions per audio block
    and the debug console, tells faults, halts and hangs apart, compares
    golden files, and writes JSON and JUnit. Its own tests: 23 cargo tests
    and a 13-case suite on 12 small test images built with the pinned
    toolchain. The suite's outputs were byte-identical in two amd64
    containers at different paths and on Apple Silicon natively.
  - **Separation**: docs/HARNESS.md (the clean side's manual) and
    docs/SPEC-REQUESTS.md; checks C-SEP-TERMS, C-CLEAN-FOLDER and

each with its source. Facts whose only source is the emulator are marked as

the key matrix, and covers what docs/HARNESS.md defers to it (the memories,

# Plan

An original, MIT-licensed base firmware for the M-VAVE FM-1 pocket
synthesizer (JieLi AC791N: two pi32v2 cores, 240x240 LCD, key matrix, rotary
encoders, I2S audio), written clean-room so it can ship inside the
F-Emulator iOS app, provably independent of the FM-1's GPL community
firmwares.

Each milestone has its own prompt (`docs/prompts/<Mx>.md`) and its own fresh
session. Roles are defined in CONTRIBUTING.md; requirement IDs are in
docs/REQUIREMENTS.md.

## Milestones

### M0a: foundation (firmware side)
Repo, rules, roles, exposure register, records, signing, toolchain, SDK, CI.
No firmware code yet; a placeholder translation unit proves the pipeline.
- Requirements: R-PROC-1..4, R-REC-1..2, R-REPRO-1..5, R-BUILD-1,
  R-LIC-1..2, R-PUB-1..2, R-CLEAN-1..5.
- Done when: the repo exists with the bootstrap commit and rulesets; CI on a
  pull request runs reuse lint, the commit-message check, the low-profile
  check, the toolchain container build with its checksum and the
  byte-for-byte double build; the owner's signed merge produces the first
  record with a pending OpenTimestamps proof; `tools/reproduce` works;
  EXPOSURE.md and PROVENANCE.md are complete; nothing forbidden was opened.
- Status 2026-10-22: pull request #1 merged as `2fd28219`. Its record
  (`records/2fd28219…/` on `records`) has 13 checks PASS and C-MERGE FAIL
  under the merge rule of the time (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Merge policy and its
  history"), with a pending OpenTimestamps proof (three calendars).
  `tools/reproduce 2fd28219` on the owner's Mac: REPRODUCED (both outputs
  match the record).

### M0b: harness (spec side)
Vendor the emulator crates `fm1-isa`, `fm1-core`, `fm1-soc` from the public
upstream `joakimeriksson/fm1-emu` at a pinned commit, with its MIT licence,
into `vendor/emulator/` (never the rest of that repo). Build the harness: a
Rust library and `fwtest` CLI that boots a raw image, runs N emulated ms with
a timed input script, captures RAM, the LCD (PNG), LEDs, flash, audio (WAV)
and instructions per audio block, detects halts, compares golden files, and
emits JUnit and JSON.
- Requirements: R-REPRO-*, R-LIC-*, new harness requirements (R-HARN-*).
- Done when: `fwtest` runs in CI from a pinned container, its outputs are
  deterministic, and `tools/clean-setup.sh` excludes `vendor/emulator/` and
  `harness/` from clean clones.
- Status 2026-10-22 (session M0b, spec side, on the owner's Mac):
  - **Setup** (pull request #3): the spec folder, its hand-made settings kept

    and the debug console, tells faults, halts and hangs apart, compares
    golden files, and writes JSON and JUnit. Its own tests: 23 cargo tests

# Hardware spec

What the spec side knows about the board, and about how fwtest presents it,
as numbered facts. It is the firmware side's only window onto that knowledge
(CONTRIBUTING.md, "Roles"). It holds facts, never code, and never how any
firmware or the emulator is written: each entry states a property of the
hardware, or a requirement it imposes, and leaves the design of the code to
the firmware side.

Written by session M0c (spec side), 2026-10-22. Ask for anything missing
through docs/SPEC-REQUESTS.md. Open spec requests at the time of writing:
none. Session SR-1-SR-2 (spec side, 2026-10-22) added sections 9 to 11 for
SR-1 and SR-2, which are answered in part; what stays open is Q-2, Q-13
and Q-14. Session SR-3 (spec side, 2026-10-23) added section 12 for SR-3,
answered in part (open: Q-6, Q-15), and section 13, which confirms HW-41's
fwtest part for M3.

## How to read it

Every fact is an entry:

- **ID**: `HW-n`. IDs are never reused or renumbered. A corrected fact gets a
  new ID, and the old entry stays, marked superseded.
- **Fact**: the property or requirement. "On the chip" means the AC791N on
  the FM-1; "in fwtest" means how fwtest presents it (docs/HARNESS.md). Where
  an entry says neither, it holds for both as far as the sources go.
- **Sources**: as precisely as possible (the keys are under "Sources" below).
- **Standing**:
  - **confirmed**: an independent source agrees: the JieLi SDK, FM-1-RE's
    documents, a datasheet, the panel sources, or a spec-side black-box
    experiment in fwtest (E-n). An experiment confirms how fwtest behaves,
    not how the chip behaves; the sources say which kind of confirmation it
    is.
  - **emulator-only**: the only source is the emulator model, which was
    partly written from GPL code. Rely on it in fwtest, but prefer to confirm
    it with your own black-box test.
  - **superseded by HW-n**: no longer true; see the newer entry.
- **Needed by**: the milestone that first needs it.

Numbers are hexadecimal with `0x`; registers are 32 bits wide and
little-endian unless an entry says otherwise. "Bit n" counts from bit 0, the
least significant. Register names are the JieLi SDK's.

## Sources

| Key | Source |
|-----|--------|
| SDK | JieLi AC79 SDK, `Jieli-Tech/fw-AC79_AIoT_SDK` (Gitee), commit `5fa84a9b2f723a5e9337ad79dc2ad741fc98fe2d`, Apache-2.0 (PROVENANCE P-2, P-10). `WL82.h` and `csfr.h` are vendored in `vendor/jieli-sdk/include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/`; the other files cited are at the same commit and path prefix. Line numbers refer to that commit. |
| RE | AL-255/FM-1-RE (GitHub, WTFPL), commit `ec832f281ca165a7d5e0722985f3acb1465046d5`: its hardware and boot documents `docs/reversing/01-hardware-map.md`, `docs/io/01-boot.md`, `docs/io/03-audio-dac.md`, `docs/io/08-display.md`, `docs/io/09-storage.md` (PROVENANCE P-9). Only their hardware facts are used here. |
| DS | Sitronix ST7789V datasheet, version 1.3 (2014-03), 316 pages, from `https://www.newhavendisplay.com/appnotes/datasheets/LCDs/ST7789V.pdf`, SHA-256 `8ecf0e43…5d04ca1` (PROVENANCE P-11). Page numbers as printed. |
| PANEL | The FM-1's printed panel labels, from two sources that agree: the owner's screenshot of the F-Emulator app's panel with its default labels, `docs/sources/panel-app-default-labels.png` (secondary: the app's drawing of the panel); and M-VAVE's product photo of the FM-1, `https://www.m-vave.com/images/products/fm-1.webp` on `https://www.m-vave.com/product.html?id=fm-1`, accessed 2026-10-22, SHA-256 `e610a746…df14b95`, not copied into this repository (PROVENANCE P-12). Only the printed labels are taken from them. The owner chose these two sources. |
| HARNESS | docs/HARNESS.md, fwtest's manual. It is the spec side's own description of fwtest, so it never confirms an entry on its own. |
| E-n | A spec-side black-box experiment: a small image run in fwtest (the pinned image, `config/fwtest-image`). Its result is stated in the entry. C-SPEC-EXPERIMENTS re-runs every one in CI, so a cited result that stops holding fails CI. |

---

## 1. The raw image and boot (M0d)
## 3. Interrupts (M1)

### HW-18: The vector table
- Fact: The handler for interrupt source n is the 32-bit address in the
  word at `0x01C7FE00 + 4 × n`, in RAM. The firmware writes the table. The
  slot of source 126 (`0x01C7FFF8`) is also core 1's start address (HW-9);
  the slot of source 127 (`0x01C7FFFC`) has no other use known here. In
  fwtest both cores use this one table.
- Sources: SDK `hwi.h` lines 114-123 (`ISR_ENTRY 0x1c7fe00`, sources up
  to 127); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §1 and §4.1; E-3, E-9: handlers
  installed this way ran.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-19: Interrupt source numbers
- Fact: The sources this spec uses: 3 core tick timer, 4-7 TIMER0-3,
  11 the audio link `JL_ALNK0` (the SDK's `IRQ_ALNK_IDX`), 16 SPI1 (LCD),
  24 SARADC, 63 TIMER5, 120-127 software interrupts 0-7. (TIMER4 is
  source 62 on the chip; it never fires in fwtest, HW-14.) The SDK's
  `hwi.h` lists the rest.
- Sources: SDK `hwi.h` lines 41-121.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-20: Enabling a source, and its priority
- Fact: Each core has its own enable and priority words, `ICFG00` to
  `ICFG31`: core 0's at `0x01EEF100` to `0x01EEF17C`, core 1's at
  `0x01EEF300` to `0x01EEF37C`. Source n uses 4 bits of word n / 8, at bit
  position 4 × (n mod 8): bit 0 enables it, bits 1-3 are its priority 0-7.
  A higher number is a higher priority. A source interrupts only the cores
  whose words enable it.
- Sources: SDK `csfr.h` lines 208-214, 280-312; SDK `hwi.h` line 135
  ("0~7, larger is higher"); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §4.1 (the 4-bit
  encoding and the two arrays); E-3, E-9 (sources enabled this way).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-21: The global interrupt gates
- Fact: A core takes interrupts only while both gates are open: bit 8 of
  its special register `icfg` (the master enable; not to be confused with
  the `ICFG00`-`ICFG31` words of HW-20) and the enable set by the
  instruction `sti` (cleared by `cli`). At entry `icfg` reads 0, so bit 8
  is clear: set it and execute `sti` before expecting interrupts.
- Sources: SDK `include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/irq.h` lines 19-21 (bit 8
  of `icfg` as the enable); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §4.1, §5.2; E-1
  (`icfg` 0 at entry); E-3 (interrupts taken after setting `icfg` bit 8
  and executing `sti`).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-22: Entering and leaving a handler, in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest, when a core takes an interrupt the address to return to
  is put in the special register `reti` and the core jumps to the handler;
  the handler returns with `rti`. A handler compiled with the toolchain's
  interrupt function attribute returns correctly. A running handler can be
  interrupted by a pending source of higher priority only after it has
  stored `reti` to its stack, and only until it loads `reti` back; sources
  of the same or lower priority wait until it returns. When several enabled
  sources are pending, the one with the highest priority is taken; between
  equal priorities the order is not specified. fwtest models only core 0's
  tick timer and software-interrupt words (HW-17, HW-23), and one vector
  table for both cores. Whether the chip behaves the same way is Q-10.
- Sources: the emulator model; E-3 and E-9 show only that handlers written
  with the toolchain's interrupt attribute run repeatedly and return.
- Standing: emulator-only
- Needed by: M1

### HW-23: Software interrupts
- Fact: Writing bit b (0-7) to `ILAT_SET` makes source 120 + b pending;
  writing bit b to `ILAT_CLR` clears it. Core 0's are at `0x01EEF1A0` and
  `0x01EEF1A4`, core 1's `0x200` higher (fwtest has core 0's only, HW-22).
  The handler must clear its source, or it is taken again on return.
- Sources: SDK `csfr.h` lines 208-214, 322-323; SDK `cpu.h` line 59 (the
  SDK raises one this way); E-3: `ILAT_SET` bit 0 ran the handler of
  source 120 once, which cleared it.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-24: Waiting for an interrupt, in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest, the instruction `idle` waits until something is due:
  time skips ahead to the next timed event, and with interrupts enabled the
  pending one is then taken. A loop that only reads TIMER4 is skipped the
  same way. Waiting therefore costs almost no instructions, and captures may
  come late while core 0 waits (HARNESS, "Time"). What `idle` does on the
  chip with interrupts masked is part of Q-10.
- Sources: HARNESS ("Time"); E-3, E-9 (main loops of `idle` woke for each
  interrupt).
- Standing: confirmed (E-3)
- Needed by: M1

## 4. The debug channel (M0d)

### HW-25: The debug message register in fwtest
- Fact: `DBG_MSG` is at `0x01EEE244` (in the `corex2` block, next to
  `DBG_WR_EN` at `0x01EEE240` and `DBG_MSG_CLR` at `0x01EEE248`). In fwtest
  each 32-bit write to `DBG_MSG` appends the word's 4 bytes, lowest first,
  to the console that `--console` saves. A byte or halfword write appends 4
  bytes too: the bytes written, merged into the word last written. Write
  whole words.
- Sources: SDK `csfr.h` lines 106-108, 136-138; HARNESS ("--console");
  E-2: word writes appended "abcd" and "12:\n"; a byte write of "X" then
  appended "X2:\n" and a halfword "YZ" appended "YZ:\n".
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-2)
- Needed by: M0d

### HW-26: Markers in RAM
- Fact: A marker word or heartbeat counter at a fixed RAM address is
  visible to fwtest through `--ram` captures and `--watchdog` (any address
  in the RAM of HW-7). On the chip, the SDK marks `DBG_MSG` read-only, so
  the console of HW-25 may not exist there (Q-5).
- Sources: HARNESS ("--ram", "--watchdog"); SDK `csfr.h` line 137
  (`___RO` `DBG_MSG`); E-1, E-3 (results read back from RAM with `--ram`;
  `--watchdog` was not exercised).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-1)
- Needed by: M0d

## 5. The LCD (M2)
- Standing: confirmed (E-7)
- Needed by: M3

## 7. Audio output (M4)

### HW-43: The audio link's registers
- Fact: `JL_ALNK0` is at `0x00012E00`: `CON0` +0, `CON1` +4, `CON2` +8,
  `CON3` +12, `ADR0` to `ADR3` at +16 to +28, `LEN` +32. Its interrupt
  source is 11.
- Sources: SDK `WL82.h` lines 664-677; SDK `hwi.h` line 50
  (`IRQ_ALNK_IDX` 11).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK)
- Needed by: M4

### HW-44: The output buffer and sample format, in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest the output plays from a buffer in RAM at the address in
  `JL_ALNK0->ADR3`: two halves, one after the other, each of `LEN` 32-bit
  words. Words alternate left, right, left, right (`LEN` / 2 stereo frames
  a half). Write each sample as a 24-bit signed value in the word's low
  bits, sign-extended: fwtest's WAV takes the whole word shifted right
  arithmetically by 8 bits, clamped to -32768..32767. Which bits the chip
  uses is Q-9.
- Sources: E-9: with `LEN` 128 each half played 64 frames; the words
  `0x007FFFFF`, `0xFF800000`, `0x01000000` and `0x00000080` came out as
  32767, -32768, 32767 and 0, and a left ramp written as value × 256 came
  out as the values; HARNESS ("audio.wav").
- Standing: confirmed (E-9)
- Needed by: M4

### HW-45: The output's rate and halves
- Fact: In fwtest, writing `JL_ALNK0->CON0` with bit 11 set starts the
  output with half 0; a half lasts `LEN` / 2 frames of 544 / 24 MHz each:
  44 117.6 frames a second (fwtest's WAV header says 44 100). Writing
  `CON0` without bit 11 stops it. `CON0` bit 15 reads the half now
  playing, so the half that has just finished, and is free to refill, is
  that bit inverted. Each finished half sets `CON2` bit 7 and raises
  interrupt source 11 (while `CON0` bit 11 is set and the source is
  enabled); writing `CON2` with bit 3 set clears it.
- Sources: E-9: with `LEN` 128, halves finished 1.451 ms apart (the first
  at 1.459 ms), the first to finish was half 0, and `CON0` bit 15 inverted
  named it each time; RE `docs/io/03-audio-dac.md` §5.3 (the meaning of
  `CON2` bit 7 and of `CON0` bit 15 in this block); HARNESS ("audio.wav").
- Standing: confirmed (RE, E-9)
- Needed by: M4

### HW-46: When fwtest takes the samples, and what it measures
- Fact: In fwtest, a half's words are read from RAM at the moment that half
  finishes playing, so they must be complete by then: refill a half while
  the other plays. `ipb.csv` has one row per finished half, with the
  instructions each core ran since the previous one (HARNESS, "Outputs").
- Sources: HARNESS ("ipb.csv"); the emulator model (when the words are
  read); E-9.
- Standing: emulator-only
- Needed by: M4

## 8. Flash storage (M7, preliminary)

Later: only what fwtest presents. M7 should ask for more through spec
requests.

### HW-47: The flash chip, in fwtest

## 9. TIMER0 to TIMER3, corrected (M1)

### HW-48: TIMER0 to TIMER3, and what the acknowledge does in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest, `JL_TIMERn->CON` bits 0-1 non-zero run timer n (n = 0
  to 3); `CON` bits 4-7 select a prescaler of the 24 MHz clock. The timer
  counts up from `CNT` and, on reaching `PRD`, raises interrupt source
  4 + n and starts again from 0. `CON` bit 15 reads 1 while pending;
  writing `CON` with bit 14 set clears it. That acknowledging write also
  restarts the count, from the value last written to `CNT` (0 after an
  interrupt), and the period from the moment of the write. So in fwtest the
  time between
  two interrupts is `PRD` prescaled counts plus the time from the interrupt
  to the write that acknowledges it: with prescaler setting 2 and `PRD`
  1500, 24 000 time-base ticks (HW-13) plus about 1 tick when the handler
  acknowledges first, and more when it acknowledges later. This is fwtest,
  not a firmware setting: the period does not depend on anything but `PRD`,
  the prescaler and where the acknowledge sits. Whether the chip restarts
  the count on the acknowledge is Q-13. On the chip, the SDK names the
  prescaler settings 0 to 15 as dividing by 1, 4, 16, 64, 2, 8, 32, 128,
  256, 1024, 4096, 16384, 512, 2048, 8192, 32768; in fwtest only setting 2
  (16) was measured (Q-3). Supersedes HW-16, which said the count starts
  again from 0 on reaching `PRD` without saying what the acknowledge does.
- Sources: SDK `hwi.h` lines 42-45 (`IRQ_TIMER0_IDX` 4 to `IRQ_TIMER3_IDX`
  7); SDK `apps/common/example/peripheral/timer/test2.c` lines 58-75 (the
  prescaler table); E-3 (the 1 ms period, `CON` read `0x8021` in the
  handler); E-13: over 100 periods, 2 400 100 ticks (24 001.0 a period)
  with the acknowledge first in the handler (1 tick after entry), and
  2 408 160 ticks (24 081.6) with it 82 ticks after entry; `CNT` read 5
  just before the acknowledge and 0 just after.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-13)
- Needed by: M1

  fwtest one `CNT` write of 115 200 bytes sends a whole frame: the screen
  shows every pixel in order.
- Sources: SDK `include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/spi.h` line 8
  (`SPI_MAX_SIZE`); SDK `apps/common/example/peripheral/spi/spi_1bit/main.c`
  line 37 (the AC791N and AC790N limits); E-16: one transfer of a whole
  frame from RAM drew it, the first and last pixels in place.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-16)
- Needed by: M2

### HW-59: SPI1's interrupt in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest `JL_SPI1->CON` reads back as last written, with bit 15
  always 1 (a transfer finishes at once) and bit 14 reading 0; before any
  write it reads `0x8000`. A transfer that finishes while bit 13 is set
  raises interrupt source 16, a DMA transfer (`CNT`) or a single byte
  (`BUF`) alike; with bit 13 clear neither raises anything. A write with
  bit 14 set acknowledges it, and sets the other bits as written: a write
  of bit 14 alone also clears bit 13. A transfer that finished with bit 13
  set stays pending until acknowledged, even if bit 13 is cleared and the
  source enabled only afterwards. This agrees with HW-29 and HW-55. It
  holds from fwtest 0.2.0; before, a `CON` write could set bits but not
  clear them, so once bit 13 had been set every later transfer raised
  source 16 (SR-3). What the chip does with a transfer that finished while
  bit 13 was clear, when bit 13 is set later, is Q-15.
- Sources: E-15: with bit 13 never set, or written clear, no interrupt
  for a DMA transfer or a byte; with it set, one for each; `CON` read
  `0x8000`, then `0xA000` while bit 13 was set; a transfer done with the
  source disabled and bit 13 then cleared was still taken once the source
  was enabled; HARNESS ("The LCD").
- Standing: confirmed (E-15)
- Needed by: M2

## 13. The SARADC's interrupt, confirmed (M3)

### HW-60: The SARADC's interrupt in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest, a conversion started (`JL_ADC->CON` written with bits
  4 and 6) with `CON` bit 5 set raises interrupt source 24 when it
  finishes, which is at once; started without bit 5 it raises nothing. In
  the handler `RES` holds the result and `CON` reads as written with bit 7
  set. Writing `CON` with bit 6 set and bit 4 clear acknowledges it; that
  write also clears bit 4, the enable, and bit 7, and the next start write
  sets bit 4 again. `CON` writes set and clear bits as written: a start
  without bit 5 after one with it raises nothing. The fwtest part of HW-41,
  now confirmed; which knob the pot is moved to HW-61.
- Sources: SDK `hwi.h` line 65 (`IRQ_SARADC_IDX` 24); E-17: one
  interrupt for each start with bit 5 and none without, `RES` 900 (the
  pot) and `CON` `0x4F0` in the handler, `0x40` after the acknowledge,
  `0x4D0` after a start without bit 5.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-17)
- Needed by: M3

### HW-61: The pot is the MASTER knob
- Fact: The pot that fwtest reads on SARADC channel 4 (HW-40), and that
  input scripts move with `pot V`, is the `MASTER` knob (HW-36). Which
  channel carries it on the chip is Q-8.
- Sources: the emulator model (which panel control the pot is); PANEL
  (the label, HW-36).
- Standing: emulator-only
- Needed by: M3

---

## Open questions

What isn't known, or is known only from material the spec may not use. A
spec request can turn one into a fact.

- **Q-1. Other RAM on the chip.** Whether the chip has RAM at `0x01F00000`

# Hardware spec

What the spec side knows about the board, and about how fwtest presents it,
as numbered facts. It is the firmware side's only window onto that knowledge
(CONTRIBUTING.md, "Roles"). It holds facts, never code, and never how any
firmware or the emulator is written: each entry states a property of the
hardware, or a requirement it imposes, and leaves the design of the code to
the firmware side.

Written by session M0c (spec side), 2026-10-22. Ask for anything missing
through docs/SPEC-REQUESTS.md. Open spec requests at the time of writing:
none. Session SR-1-SR-2 (spec side, 2026-10-22) added sections 9 to 11 for
SR-1 and SR-2, which are answered in part; what stays open is Q-2, Q-13
and Q-14. Session SR-3 (spec side, 2026-10-23) added section 12 for SR-3,
answered in part (open: Q-6, Q-15), and section 13, which confirms HW-41's
fwtest part for M3.

## How to read it

Every fact is an entry:

- **ID**: `HW-n`. IDs are never reused or renumbered. A corrected fact gets a
  new ID, and the old entry stays, marked superseded.
- **Fact**: the property or requirement. "On the chip" means the AC791N on
  the FM-1; "in fwtest" means how fwtest presents it (docs/HARNESS.md). Where
  an entry says neither, it holds for both as far as the sources go.
- **Sources**: as precisely as possible (the keys are under "Sources" below).
- **Standing**:
  - **confirmed**: an independent source agrees: the JieLi SDK, FM-1-RE's
    documents, a datasheet, the panel sources, or a spec-side black-box
    experiment in fwtest (E-n). An experiment confirms how fwtest behaves,
    not how the chip behaves; the sources say which kind of confirmation it
    is.
  - **emulator-only**: the only source is the emulator model, which was
    partly written from GPL code. Rely on it in fwtest, but prefer to confirm
    it with your own black-box test.
  - **superseded by HW-n**: no longer true; see the newer entry.
- **Needed by**: the milestone that first needs it.

Numbers are hexadecimal with `0x`; registers are 32 bits wide and
little-endian unless an entry says otherwise. "Bit n" counts from bit 0, the
least significant. Register names are the JieLi SDK's.

## 3. Interrupts (M1)

### HW-18: The vector table
- Fact: The handler for interrupt source n is the 32-bit address in the
  word at `0x01C7FE00 + 4 × n`, in RAM. The firmware writes the table. The
  slot of source 126 (`0x01C7FFF8`) is also core 1's start address (HW-9);
  the slot of source 127 (`0x01C7FFFC`) has no other use known here. In
  fwtest both cores use this one table.
- Sources: SDK `hwi.h` lines 114-123 (`ISR_ENTRY 0x1c7fe00`, sources up
  to 127); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §1 and §4.1; E-3, E-9: handlers
  installed this way ran.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-19: Interrupt source numbers
- Fact: The sources this spec uses: 3 core tick timer, 4-7 TIMER0-3,
  11 the audio link `JL_ALNK0` (the SDK's `IRQ_ALNK_IDX`), 16 SPI1 (LCD),
  24 SARADC, 63 TIMER5, 120-127 software interrupts 0-7. (TIMER4 is
  source 62 on the chip; it never fires in fwtest, HW-14.) The SDK's
  `hwi.h` lists the rest.
- Sources: SDK `hwi.h` lines 41-121.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-20: Enabling a source, and its priority
- Fact: Each core has its own enable and priority words, `ICFG00` to
  `ICFG31`: core 0's at `0x01EEF100` to `0x01EEF17C`, core 1's at
  `0x01EEF300` to `0x01EEF37C`. Source n uses 4 bits of word n / 8, at bit
  position 4 × (n mod 8): bit 0 enables it, bits 1-3 are its priority 0-7.
  A higher number is a higher priority. A source interrupts only the cores
  whose words enable it.
- Sources: SDK `csfr.h` lines 208-214, 280-312; SDK `hwi.h` line 135
  ("0~7, larger is higher"); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §4.1 (the 4-bit
  encoding and the two arrays); E-3, E-9 (sources enabled this way).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-21: The global interrupt gates
- Fact: A core takes interrupts only while both gates are open: bit 8 of
  its special register `icfg` (the master enable; not to be confused with
  the `ICFG00`-`ICFG31` words of HW-20) and the enable set by the
  instruction `sti` (cleared by `cli`). At entry `icfg` reads 0, so bit 8
  is clear: set it and execute `sti` before expecting interrupts.
- Sources: SDK `include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/irq.h` lines 19-21 (bit 8
  of `icfg` as the enable); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §4.1, §5.2; E-1
  (`icfg` 0 at entry); E-3 (interrupts taken after setting `icfg` bit 8
  and executing `sti`).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-22: Entering and leaving a handler, in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest, when a core takes an interrupt the address to return to
  is put in the special register `reti` and the core jumps to the handler;
  the handler returns with `rti`. A handler compiled with the toolchain's
  interrupt function attribute returns correctly. A running handler can be
  interrupted by a pending source of higher priority only after it has
  stored `reti` to its stack, and only until it loads `reti` back; sources
  of the same or lower priority wait until it returns. When several enabled
  sources are pending, the one with the highest priority is taken; between
  equal priorities the order is not specified. fwtest models only core 0's
  tick timer and software-interrupt words (HW-17, HW-23), and one vector
  table for both cores. Whether the chip behaves the same way is Q-10.
- Sources: the emulator model; E-3 and E-9 show only that handlers written
  with the toolchain's interrupt attribute run repeatedly and return.
- Standing: emulator-only
- Needed by: M1

### HW-23: Software interrupts
- Fact: Writing bit b (0-7) to `ILAT_SET` makes source 120 + b pending;
  writing bit b to `ILAT_CLR` clears it. Core 0's are at `0x01EEF1A0` and
  `0x01EEF1A4`, core 1's `0x200` higher (fwtest has core 0's only, HW-22).
  The handler must clear its source, or it is taken again on return.
- Sources: SDK `csfr.h` lines 208-214, 322-323; SDK `cpu.h` line 59 (the
  SDK raises one this way); E-3: `ILAT_SET` bit 0 ran the handler of
  source 120 once, which cleared it.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-3)
- Needed by: M1

### HW-24: Waiting for an interrupt, in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest, the instruction `idle` waits until something is due:
  time skips ahead to the next timed event, and with interrupts enabled the
  pending one is then taken. A loop that only reads TIMER4 is skipped the
  same way. Waiting therefore costs almost no instructions, and captures may
  come late while core 0 waits (HARNESS, "Time"). What `idle` does on the
  chip with interrupts masked is part of Q-10.
- Sources: HARNESS ("Time"); E-3, E-9 (main loops of `idle` woke for each
  interrupt).
- Standing: confirmed (E-3)
- Needed by: M1

## 9. TIMER0 to TIMER3, corrected (M1)

### HW-48: TIMER0 to TIMER3, and what the acknowledge does in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest, `JL_TIMERn->CON` bits 0-1 non-zero run timer n (n = 0
  to 3); `CON` bits 4-7 select a prescaler of the 24 MHz clock. The timer
  counts up from `CNT` and, on reaching `PRD`, raises interrupt source
  4 + n and starts again from 0. `CON` bit 15 reads 1 while pending;
  writing `CON` with bit 14 set clears it. That acknowledging write also
  restarts the count, from the value last written to `CNT` (0 after an
  interrupt), and the period from the moment of the write. So in fwtest the
  time between
  two interrupts is `PRD` prescaled counts plus the time from the interrupt
  to the write that acknowledges it: with prescaler setting 2 and `PRD`
  1500, 24 000 time-base ticks (HW-13) plus about 1 tick when the handler
  acknowledges first, and more when it acknowledges later. This is fwtest,
  not a firmware setting: the period does not depend on anything but `PRD`,
  the prescaler and where the acknowledge sits. Whether the chip restarts
  the count on the acknowledge is Q-13. On the chip, the SDK names the
  prescaler settings 0 to 15 as dividing by 1, 4, 16, 64, 2, 8, 32, 128,
  256, 1024, 4096, 16384, 512, 2048, 8192, 32768; in fwtest only setting 2
  (16) was measured (Q-3). Supersedes HW-16, which said the count starts
  again from 0 on reaching `PRD` without saying what the acknowledge does.
- Sources: SDK `hwi.h` lines 42-45 (`IRQ_TIMER0_IDX` 4 to `IRQ_TIMER3_IDX`
  7); SDK `apps/common/example/peripheral/timer/test2.c` lines 58-75 (the
  prescaler table); E-3 (the 1 ms period, `CON` read `0x8021` in the
  handler); E-13: over 100 periods, 2 400 100 ticks (24 001.0 a period)
  with the acknowledge first in the handler (1 tick after entry), and
  2 408 160 ticks (24 081.6) with it 82 ticks after entry; `CNT` read 5
  just before the acknowledge and 0 just after.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-13)
- Needed by: M1

  fwtest one `CNT` write of 115 200 bytes sends a whole frame: the screen
  shows every pixel in order.
- Sources: SDK `include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm/spi.h` line 8

  frame from RAM drew it, the first and last pixels in place.
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, E-16)
- Needed by: M2

### HW-59: SPI1's interrupt in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest `JL_SPI1->CON` reads back as last written, with bit 15
  always 1 (a transfer finishes at once) and bit 14 reading 0; before any
  write it reads `0x8000`. A transfer that finishes while bit 13 is set
  raises interrupt source 16, a DMA transfer (`CNT`) or a single byte
  (`BUF`) alike; with bit 13 clear neither raises anything. A write with
  bit 14 set acknowledges it, and sets the other bits as written: a write
  of bit 14 alone also clears bit 13. A transfer that finished with bit 13
  set stays pending until acknowledged, even if bit 13 is cleared and the
  source enabled only afterwards. This agrees with HW-29 and HW-55. It
  holds from fwtest 0.2.0; before, a `CON` write could set bits but not
  clear them, so once bit 13 had been set every later transfer raised
  source 16 (SR-3). What the chip does with a transfer that finished while
  bit 13 was clear, when bit 13 is set later, is Q-15.

  source disabled and bit 13 then cleared was still taken once the source
  was enabled; HARNESS ("The LCD").

  probe on real hardware.

  table (HW-48); fwtest's settings other than 0 and 2 were not measured.
  Measure with a black-box test, or ask.

  counts on real hardware (fwtest always uses 10 ms).

  anywhere on real hardware (the SDK marks it read-only, and reads it as
  the exception's cause word, HW-51), or which UART pins could carry debug

  carry on the board (fwtest gives them fixed values).

# fwtest: the harness, as a black box

`fwtest` runs a raw image on an emulated board for a given number of
emulated milliseconds, feeds it timed inputs, and saves what it did:
memory, the screen, the LEDs, the flash chip, the audio, instruction counts.
It is the firmware side's only window into the emulator, and this page is
its whole manual. It says what fwtest does, not how the emulator does it.
Facts about the chip itself (registers, pins, timings, the panel's layout)
belong in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`; ask for one through docs/SPEC-REQUESTS.md.

fwtest is a model. Where it and `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` disagree, the spec is the
authority on the hardware; report the difference as a spec request.

## Running it

The firmware side runs fwtest only through `tools/fwtest`, which runs the
published container image pinned by digest in `config/fwtest-image`
(R-SEP-3). It needs Docker; the image runs as linux/amd64 on any host.

```sh
tools/fwtest run out/build/app.bin --ms 100 --out out/t1 --ram 0x01c00000:64@end
tools/fwtest suite tests/fw/boot.suite --out out/suite
tools/fwtest version
tools/fwtest --image        # the pinned image reference
```

- Run it from the repository root. The current folder is mounted read-only,
  so every input path (image, script, flash file, golden folder, suite) must
  be inside it. `--out` is created and mounted writable on its own, and must
  be empty or not exist yet.
- The container has no network and runs as your user.
- After a run, `tools/fwtest` adds `runner.txt` to the output folder, naming
  the image it ran and whether it was the pinned one. A test record that
  used fwtest names that image; every record also notes the pinned image in
  its environment.

## The raw image

| Rule | Value |
|------|-------|
| Format | A flat binary: the bytes of the code window, from its first byte. No header, no ELF. |
| Load address | The image's first byte is at `0x02000000`, the start of the code window. Link it there. |
| Entry | Core 0 starts at `0x02000000`: the image's first instruction. |
| Size | 1 byte to 1 032 192 bytes (1 MiB less 16 KiB). |
| The flash chip | 1 MiB. Erased (all `0xFF`) unless `--flash FILE` gives its first bytes. The image is then written into it at offset `0x4000`, as an installed image sits. |
| Past the image | Reads in the code window after the image's last byte show the flash chip: window address `0x02000000 + n` shows chip offset `0x4000 + n`. Changes the image makes to the chip (erase, program) show through the window, also over the image's own bytes. |
| Writes to the window | Ignored (and listed as unmodelled accesses). |
| RAM | 1 MiB at `0x01C00000`, all zero at the start. Other memories, and what the real chip has: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| Core 0 at the start | User mode. Every register is 0, both stack pointers included (set your own stacks first), except `r0` = `0x01C7FC00`: a 64-byte block of zeros whose first word holds `0x01C7FC40`. |
| Core 1 | Does not run until the image releases it (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md` says how). Then it runs alongside core 0. |

## Time

- Emulated time starts at 0 when the image starts. One instruction of core 0
  takes one cycle; there are 240 000 cycles in an emulated millisecond.
- Everything happens at exact emulated times, and the outputs are
  deterministic (below), but **while core 0 waits, fwtest moves time ahead**,
  so that waiting costs (almost) no instructions and instruction counts
  measure work. The rules for that, and what they do to captures, are
  exact; they follow.

### When fwtest treats core 0 as waiting

Two things, and nothing else, count as waiting:

1. **The wait-for-interrupt instruction**, executed by core 0 while no
   interrupt is pending. Time jumps to one cycle before the next scheduled
   event (below). With nothing scheduled, time doesn't jump.
2. **Polling the free-running timer**: reading its count (HW-13 in
   `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, the 24 MHz time base), outside an interrupt handler
   of core 0, for the third time or more in a row with each read coming
   within 64 cycles (64 instructions of core 0) of the one before. On each
   such read, time jumps ahead by up to 20 µs, and never past one cycle
   before the next scheduled event. The read then returns the count for
   the new time.
   - **Only the spacing of the reads matters.** What the loop does between
     them doesn't: stores to RAM, arithmetic, reads of other registers, a
     call. A loop that reads the count every few instructions *and* writes
     a heartbeat to RAM on every pass is waiting, by this rule.
   - A read more than 64 cycles after the previous one starts the count
     again, so a loop whose reads are at least 64 instructions apart is
     never treated as waiting.
   - Reads made while core 0 is in an interrupt handler are ignored: they
     neither count, nor jump, nor break a sequence.
   - Reads by core 1 count in the same sequence as core 0's: the rule
     looks at reads of the count, not at which core made them.
   - Other timers' counters, their pending flags, and RAM flags are not
     part of this rule. Polling them never moves time ahead.

**Scheduled events** are what the emulated chip and the script have coming
next:
- the end of a timer period;
- an audio half-buffer finishing;
- a transfer completing;
- a MIDI byte arriving;
- an encoder contact changing;
- a script event.

They count whether or not their interrupt is enabled. **Captures, the end
of the run and the watchdog are not scheduled events:** a jump never stops
for them.

### What that does to captures

- fwtest looks at the board between runs of core 0 instructions. Each run
  is at most 1024 instructions, and no longer than the instructions that
  would reach the next capture (or the end of the run) at one cycle each.
  Captures, the watchdog, halts and the end of the run are checked only
  between runs. A capture is taken at the first such stop at or after its
  time.
- **While core 0 is busy (not waiting), captures are exact:** taken at the
  first instruction boundary at or after the time asked.
- **While core 0 waits, a capture can come late**, because every jump
  inside a run moves time without using up the run's instructions:
  - Polling the timer: each read can add up to 20 µs. A loop that reads the
    count every *k* instructions can move up to about 1024 / *k* × 20 µs in
    one run, for example 2 ms when *k* is 10. A capture asked for at *t*
    can be taken that much after *t*.
  - Wait-for-interrupt: each wait jumps to the next scheduled event. A run
    that wakes on every event can cross many of them, for example several
    milliseconds of 100 µs interrupts.
- What is late is the moment the capture is taken, not its label. RAM and
  screen captures show the state at the moment fwtest took them, but are
  named for the time asked (`ram-…-10ms.bin`). `leds.csv`'s `ms` column is
  the time asked, while each duty value covers the real time since the
  previous sample. The end of the run, and so every `end` capture, can come
  late in the same way. `result.json`'s `emulated_ms` says when the run
  really ended.
- The watchdog compares its word between runs, so a hang is noticed up to
  one run late.
- None of this varies between runs: the same image, script and options give
  the same late times, byte for byte, everywhere.

### Getting exact timing

- **Don't wait around the times you capture.** Keep core 0 busy then, for
  example by spacing reads of the timer's count at least 64 instructions
  apart, or by waiting on something else: another timer's pending flag, or
  a RAM flag that an interrupt handler sets. Captures are then exact.
- **Or let the image record the time itself.** Store the timer's count (or
  your own tick count) next to what you capture, and check the capture
  against that stored time instead of the time asked. The M0d firmware's
  beacon does this (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md).
- **For the end of a run**, read `emulated_ms` in `result.json`.
- Instruction counts (`instructions` in `result.json`, `ipb.csv`) do not
  include the time jumped over: a waiting image's counts stay small and
  stable.

### Timers and their acknowledge

The write to a TIMER0 to TIMER3 control register that acknowledges its
interrupt also restarts that timer's count and its period from the moment
of the write. So the time between two of its interrupts is the
period programmed plus the time from the interrupt to the acknowledging
write: about one tick of the 24 MHz time base when the handler acknowledges
first, more when it acknowledges later (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-48). To
measure a period exactly, acknowledge first, or subtract the time the
handler took to reach its acknowledge. Whether the chip does the same is an
open question in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`.

## The LCD

The panel's transfers finish at once: SPI1's done bit always reads 1, and
a DMA transfer of any length up to a whole screen in one `CNT` write
(115 200 bytes) draws (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-29, HW-58). SPI1's `CON`
reads back as last written. A transfer, by DMA or a single byte, that
finishes while `CON` bit 13 is set raises interrupt source 16; with bit 13
clear it raises nothing. A write with bit 14 set acknowledges it, and like
every write it sets the other bits as written: a write of bit 14 alone also
clears bit 13. A transfer that finished with bit 13 set stays pending until
acknowledged, even if bit 13 is cleared afterwards (HW-59).

From fwtest 0.2.0. Before it, a write to `CON` could set bits but never
clear them: once any write had set bit 13, every later transfer raised
source 16, whatever `CON` was written to afterwards (SR-3).

## The command line

```
fwtest run IMAGE --ms MS --out DIR [options]
fwtest suite FILE --out DIR
fwtest version
```

`run` options:

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `--ms MS` | Run for MS emulated milliseconds (up to three decimals). Required. |
| `--out DIR` | Write the outputs here. Required; must be empty or new. |
| `--script FILE` | Timed inputs (below). |
| `--flash FILE` | The flash chip's first bytes (at most 1 MiB); the rest is erased. |
| `--ram ADDR:LEN@WHEN` | Save LEN bytes of memory at ADDR at WHEN. Numbers in decimal, or hex with `0x`. Only RAM (main RAM and the other RAM banks `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` lists) can be saved; anything else is a usage error. Repeatable. |
| `--lcd WHEN` | Save the screen as a PNG at WHEN. Repeatable. |
| `--leds-every MS` | Sample the LEDs every MS into `leds.csv`. |
| `--flash-out` | Save the whole flash chip at the end (`flash.bin`). |
| `--wav` | Save the audio output (`audio.wav`). |
| `--ipb` | Save instructions per audio block (`ipb.csv`). |
| `--console` | Save the bytes written to the chip's debug message register (`console.txt`; `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` names it). |
| `--watchdog ADDR:MS` | A hang if the 32-bit word at RAM address ADDR stays the same for more than MS ms. |
| `--halt-ok` | A halt counts as success (exit 0). |
| `--golden DIR` | Compare the outputs with the golden files in DIR (below). |

WHEN is a time in ms (`10`, `2.5`) or `end`. The run ends at `--ms`, or
earlier on a fault, halt or hang; `end` captures are taken then.

## Input scripts

A text file, one event per line; `#` starts a comment. Times are emulated
milliseconds with up to three decimals. Events at the same time happen in
the order written.

```
# time   event
2        key 12 down
4        key 12 up
6        key 5 tap 3          # down at 6 ms, up at 9 ms (default hold: 50 ms)
10       enc 0 +2             # encoder 0, two detents clockwise
12       enc 3 -1             # one detent anticlockwise
15       pot 300              # the pot now reads 300
20       midi 90 3c 64        # bytes into the MIDI input, in this order
```

| Event | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `key N down`, `key N up` | Key N (0 to 40) pressed or released. |
| `key N tap [HOLD]` | Pressed, then released HOLD ms later (default 50). |
| `enc N +C`, `enc N -C` | Encoder N (0 to 6) turned C detents (1 to 1000); `+` is clockwise. Each detent is four contact changes, 2 ms apart, the first at the event's time. |
| `pot V` | The pot's reading becomes V (0 to 1023). It reads 900 until a script sets it. |
| `midi HH ...` | Bytes (two hex digits each) arrive at the MIDI input one after another, at the wire's pace: one byte every 320 µs, the first 320 µs after the event's time. |

Key, LED and encoder numbers are fwtest's own. `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` maps them
to the panel and to the key matrix.

## Outputs

All in `--out`. A run writes only what it was asked for, plus
`result.json` and `junit.xml`.

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `ram-AAAAAAAA-L-WHEN.bin` | The bytes saved by `--ram` (address as 8 hex digits, length in hex, WHEN as `10ms`, `2.500ms` or `end`). |
| `lcd-WHEN.png` | The screen, 240 x 240, 8-bit RGB, whatever the display's on/off state. Each pixel is the panel's 16-bit colour (5-6-5 bits) with each channel scaled to 8 bits (`c * 255 / 31`, or `/ 63` for green). |
| `leds.csv` | Header `ms,led0,...,led40`, then one row per sample: the sample's time, and for each LED the share of the time since the previous sample (or since the start) that it was lit, in thousandths (0 to 1000, rounded). LED N belongs to key N. |
| `flash.bin` | The flash chip (1 MiB) at the end of the run. |
| `audio.wav` | The audio output: 16-bit PCM, stereo, the header says 44 100 Hz. Every sample the output played, in order. How the firmware feeds the output, and its exact rate: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| `ipb.csv` | Header `block,end_ms,core0,core1`, then one row per audio block (each time the output finished one half of its buffer): its number, the time it finished, and the instructions core 0 and core 1 executed since the previous block (the first row: since the start). Core 0's count is exact; core 1's is counted at a granularity of 1024 core-0 instructions. |
| `console.txt` | The debug console bytes, as written. |
| `result.json` | What happened (below). |
| `junit.xml` | JUnit XML: a test case `run` (fails on a fault or hang, and on a halt without `--halt-ok`), and one `golden NAME` per golden file. |

`result.json` holds: `fwtest` (version and the emulator build it carries),
`image` (file name, size, SHA-256), `script_sha256`, `run` (`outcome`,
`detail`, `emulated_ms`, `instructions` per core, `midi_bytes_dropped`,
`unmodelled_accesses`, and every output's name, size and SHA-256), `golden`
(each file's `match` or `mismatch` and why), and `exit_code`.

- `midi_bytes_dropped`: bytes that arrived while the image had no MIDI
  receiver set up, or more than about a second's worth waiting.
- `unmodelled_accesses`: addresses the image read or wrote that fwtest does
  not model (reads give 0, writes are dropped), with counts, up to 256.
  Usually a sign the image touched something unexpected; if the hardware
  has something there, ask for it in a spec request.

## Outcomes and exit codes

| Exit | Outcome | When |
|------|---------|------|
| 0 | completed | Ran for `--ms`, and every golden file matched. (Also a halt with `--halt-ok`.) |
| 1 | golden mismatch | A golden file differs (beyond its tolerance), or an output it names is missing. |
| 2 | usage error | Bad arguments, an unreadable or oversized image, a bad script, `--out` not empty, a capture outside RAM. Nothing ran. |
| 3 | fault | A core met an instruction it cannot decode or the emulator does not implement, or its program counter left every memory that can hold code (the image, RAM, the other RAM banks). |
| 4 | halt | Core 0 executed a jump to itself with interrupts disabled: a deliberate stop. The run ends there. |
| 5 | hang | The `--watchdog` word did not change for longer than its time. |

When several apply, the first in this order wins: 2, 3, 5, 1, 4, 0. Captures
and `result.json` are written for 1, 3, 4 and 5 too. Any other exit code
means fwtest itself failed.

### Faults and CPU exceptions

fwtest raises no CPU exception: no condition makes interrupt source 0, 1
or 2 pending, so an image's exception handler is never entered by a fault.
What happens instead (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-52, says it with the measured
values):

- Misaligned loads and stores complete. A word load or store uses the 4
  bytes at the address given; a halfword load from an odd RAM address
  ignores the lowest address bit.
- Reads outside every memory and register fwtest models give 0, writes
  there are dropped, and both are listed in `unmodelled_accesses`; so are
  writes to the code window, which are dropped too.
- A division by zero gives 0.
- An instruction fwtest cannot decode ends the run as a fault (exit 3).
  fwtest may stop at the start of the straight-line code that holds it,
  before any of that code has run, and `result.json` then gives that
  address as the fault's `pc`; to have code run up to it, put the
  instruction behind a call or a branch.
- A jump outside every memory runs what fwtest reads there (zeros) for up to
  1024 instructions, until fwtest next checks the program counter, and then
  ends the run as a fault.

## Golden files

`--golden DIR`: every file in DIR is a golden file, compared with the output
of the same name. A golden file without such an output is a mismatch. Outputs
without a golden file are not compared.

- **Exact by default:** byte for byte. Every fwtest output is deterministic,
  so exact is right unless the firmware's own behaviour is meant to vary.
- **Tolerances**, where an output is meant to be approximate: a text file
  `NAME.tolerance` beside the golden file, one line:
  - `pixel-diff N` (a `.png`): same size; each colour channel of each pixel
    within N.
  - `sample-diff N` (a `.wav`): same format and length; each sample within N.
  - `rel-percent P` (a `.csv`): same lines and fields; text fields equal;
    each integer within P percent of the golden value (at least 1). For
    example `ipb.csv` with `rel-percent 3` is the performance gate R-PERF-2
    will use.
- Golden PNG and WAV files compared with a tolerance must be ones fwtest
  wrote. To make a golden file, run once, check the output by hand, and copy
  it into the golden folder in the same commit as the test.

## Suites

`fwtest suite FILE --out DIR` runs several cases. Each line of FILE:

```
# NAME  EXPECT     IMAGE                 run options (paths relative to FILE)
boot    completed  ../out/build/app.bin  --ms 50 --ram 0x01c00000:16@end --golden golden/boot
stop    halt       images/stop.bin       --ms 10
```

NAME (letters, digits, `-`, `_`) is the case's output folder under DIR.
EXPECT is the outcome expected: `completed`, `halt`, `fault` or `hang`. A
case passes when its outcome is EXPECT and every golden file matches. DIR
also gets `result.json` (every case's result) and `junit.xml` (one test case
per suite case). The exit code is 0 when every case passes, 1 otherwise, 2
on a usage error.

## Determinism

The same image, script, options and fwtest build give byte-identical outputs
on every run and every machine: no host time, no randomness that isn't
seeded the same way every run, nothing from the environment, no host paths
in the results. CI runs the harness's own suite twice in fresh containers
and compares every output byte (C-HARNESS-DET). If two runs of yours ever
differ, that is a bug in fwtest: report it.

## Versions

`fwtest version` prints fwtest's version and the emulator build it carries;
`result.json` has both. The image is identified by its digest. When the
harness changes, a pull request moves `config/fwtest-image` to the new
digest, so a firmware test always names the exact runner it used.

- 0.2.0: SPI1's `CON` writes set and clear bits as written ("The LCD").
- 0.1.0: the first published image.
